---
title: "Weighted hydrographs for Montana brown trout"
subtitle: "When does water help, by how much, and what do the forecasts imply?"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source("_common.R")
```

## The question

Reclamation and its partners can move water, but not much of it and not whenever
they like. The operational question is not whether trout like water. It is
**when** a given volume does the most good, and what the flow futures already in
the models imply for populations that are managed on that basis.

Most flow-ecology work answers a related but different question, because it
collapses the hydrograph before analysing it: summer mean discharge, peak
magnitude, days below a threshold. Every one of those summaries is a hypothesis
about when flow matters, chosen before looking at the data. This analysis does
not collapse the hydrograph. It estimates a coefficient for **every day of the
year**.

## What a weighted hydrograph is

For each year *i*, with `x_i(t)` the standardized discharge anomaly on day *t*:

$$ y_i = a + \sum_{t=1}^{365} \beta(t)\, x_i(t) + \varepsilon_i $$

$\beta(t)$ is the weighted hydrograph: how much a wet day on 3 August is
worth compared with a wet day on 3 March. Score any hydrograph with it - an
observed year, a forecast, a proposed release - and the sum is the predicted
change in the response.

The seasonal-average model is a special case of this: $\beta(t)$ constant
inside the season and zero outside. So this framework can *test* whether a
seasonal covariate was looking in the right place, instead of assuming it.

## How to read this site

```{r nav, results='asis'}
cat("- **[Methods](methods.html)** - how beta(t) is estimated, validated, and converted into cfs.\n",
    "- **[Results by site](results.html)** - a dropdown and one row per population. Start here.\n",
    "- **[Among sites](results_among_sites.html)** - what the daily curves say across Montana.\n\n", sep = "")
```

**Read the gate before the figures.** Every per-site page opens with it. The
arithmetic produces a curve whether or not the record supports one; the gate is
what separates a finding from a shape. A site that fails is a result about the
resolution of Montana flow records, and it is reported as such rather than
quietly dropped.

## The honest limits

- **About 40 years against 365 days.** Seasonal statements are usually
  supportable; single days often are not. Each site page reports the width of the
  best-day interval and says outright when a season is the finest honest claim.
- **The estimator can only build beta(t) from the leading modes of variation in
  flow,** which are chosen without looking at the response. A signal living in a
  low-variance flow mode cannot appear in the curve, however real it is.
- **The gate tests prediction, not causation.** A curve that passes predicts
  years the model did not see. It does not identify the mechanism, and the
  mechanism is what a flow recommendation ultimately rests on.
- **Scenario effects are measured against the observed gage climatology,** not
  against the forecast model's own historical run. Hydrologic model bias at a
  site is therefore reported as a climate effect.
